activity_context.topic_title: Reducing Real 2x2 Matrices to Rotation-Scaling Form

examples.knowledge_point: Converting a Matrix to Rotation-Scaling Form Given Only One Eigenvalue
examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14071601/assets/74cc68e763183d4599dc223cce44849ace88129bbc82b6d49bcbafc4a1a8163d.png)
Consider the matrices shown above.
Given that $A$ has the complex eigenvalue $\lambda=-2+6\textrm{i},$ and that $A=PCP^{-1}$ where $C$ is a rotation-scaling matrix, find the matrix $P.$
examples.worked_solution:
Recall that for any $2 \times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PCP^{-1},$ where 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14071601/assets/b5c1766ea1d9eb7a913fd7be2d7bf71909c81da03aaff8f4c631e1a3955f9589.png)

and $\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue  $\lambda.$

Since we are given the eigenvalue $\lambda=-2+6\textrm{i},$ we can immediately construct the rotation-scaling matrix:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14071601/assets/7f29c1c9be88268b14ef9131599420874fff6a399a3e3c92d3f4b635906163f6.png)

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions to the matrix equation 

$$
(A - \lambda I) \textbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda_1 =-2+6\textrm{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -5 \\ 9 & -5\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-2+6\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -2+6\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3-6\text{i} & -5 \\ 9 & -3-6\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(3-6\text{i}){x}_{1}-5{x}_{2}=0 \\ 9{x}_{1}+(-3-6\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the matrix $A-\lambda I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
x_1=\dfrac 1 3(1+2\textrm{i})x_2.
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14071601/assets/ab958a638d0bce3cb2498d6f64016e581bb303fd0df725abcfaa58dbd836b95d.png)

Setting $x_2=3$, we get the eigenvector 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14071601/assets/631f718ed2642536c5a8e02dedc38544af5e8b6cc48bff7a0afcf77c0d057d1b.png)

Therefore, we can construct the matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem:
$$
v=[\begin{aligned}3+2\text{i} \\ 2\text{i}\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ -3 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the vector $v$ and the rotation-scaling matrix $C$ shown above. Given that $v$ is an eigenvector of a $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2-3\text{i},$ find a matrix $P$ such that $A=PC{P}^{-1}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall that for any $2\times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ where 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}],
$$

and $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue  $\lambda .$

First, notice that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -3 \\ 3 & -2\end{aligned}]\ne C,
$$

while

$$
[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\overset{―}{\lambda }) & \text{Im}(\overset{―}{\lambda }) \\ -\text{Im}(\overset{―}{\lambda }) & \text{Re}(\overset{―}{\lambda })\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ -3 & -2\end{aligned}]=C.
$$

So, our rotation-scaling matrix $C$ corresponds to the eigenvalue $\overset{―}{\lambda }=-2+3\text{i},$ 
 the complex conjugate of $\lambda .$ Hence, to construct the matrix $P,$ we use the eigenvector $\overset{―}{v},$ the complex conjugate of $v.$

Next, we find the real and imaginary parts of our eigenvector:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{v} & =[\begin{aligned}3-2\text{i} \\ -2\text{i}\end{aligned}]={{[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Re}(\overset{―}{v})}+\text{i}{{[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Im}(\overset{―}{v})}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can now construct $P:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(\overset{―}{v}) & \text{Im}(\overset{―}{v}) \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
